difficultyReason: The argument hinges on a subtle temporal gap: the policy was enacted before the data shift, but the necessary assumption concerns whether a confounding variable—not the policy—explains the improvement. Negation test requires close re-reading of the causal chain.
stimulus: City health official: After the municipal water-fluoridation program was expanded three years ago, the rate of tooth decay among children in this city fell by 22 percent. No other city-wide dental health initiative was launched during that period. Therefore, the expansion of the fluoridation program was responsible for the decline in tooth decay.
questionStem: The health official's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fluoridation program is the most cost-effective dental health intervention available to the city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rate of tooth decay among adults in the city did not decline over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No factor other than the expanded fluoridation program accounts for the observed decline in tooth decay among children.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fluoridated water reduces tooth decay in children more effectively than fluoridated toothpaste does.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The children whose tooth decay rates were measured were the same children throughout the three-year period.

explanations.correct: The official infers causation from correlation, ruling out only other city-wide initiatives. But dietary changes, improved school dental programs, or demographic shifts could explain the decline. Negate C—some other factor does account for the decline—and the fluoridation program is no longer the established cause. The conclusion collapses, so C is necessary.
explanations.A: Cost-effectiveness is irrelevant to whether the program caused the observed decline. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Adult decay rates are not part of the reasoning about children's decay. Shift in subject trap.
explanations.D: The comparison to toothpaste is never invoked in the argument; this introduces an external comparison not required for the causal conclusion.
explanations.E: The argument is about population-level rates, not the same individual children; whether the same cohort was tracked does not determine whether the program caused the decline.

difficultyReason: The chronological subtlety—whether the inscription was added at the time of composition or later—is easy to miss on a first read. The necessary assumption concerns the provenance of the manuscript evidence, not the content of the inscription itself.
stimulus: Historian: A manuscript discovered in a Florentine archive bears an inscription attributing it to a scribe who died in 1423. The manuscript's parchment has been dated by chemical analysis to between 1400 and 1440. Scholars have therefore concluded that the manuscript was produced during the scribe's lifetime.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the scholars' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The scribe named in the inscription produced other manuscripts that survive to this day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inscription attributing the manuscript to the scribe was not added to the parchment after the scribe's death.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chemical dating of parchment is the most reliable method of establishing a manuscript's age.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No manuscripts produced in Florence before 1400 have survived into the present day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Florentine archive acquired the manuscript before any alterations could be made to it.

explanations.correct: The argument uses the inscription as evidence that the scribe produced the manuscript. But if the inscription was added after the scribe's death—say, as a false attribution—the parchment date merely tells us when the parchment was made, not who wrote on it. Negate B: the inscription was added after the scribe's death. Then the conclusion that the manuscript was produced during his lifetime is unsupported. B is necessary.
explanations.A: The existence of other manuscripts by the scribe is irrelevant to whether this particular manuscript was produced during his lifetime.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't require chemical dating to be the most reliable method—only that the dating result here is accurate enough to draw the conclusion. Too strong/comparative trap.
explanations.D: The survival of pre-1400 manuscripts is wholly unrelated to dating this manuscript.
explanations.E: Archive acquisition history is out of scope; alterations before archive entry are what matter, and the argument doesn't invoke the archive's custodial record.

difficultyReason: The argument involves a conditional inference about software security. The necessary assumption is a narrow defender—ruling out a specific alternative pathway for the breach—rather than a broad causal claim. Distractors are carefully calibrated to sound like gap-fillers without passing the negation test.
stimulus: Security analyst: Access to the company's proprietary database requires both a valid employee credential and a device registered on the internal network. The breach that occurred last month exposed customer records stored in that database. Since none of the company's registered devices were reported stolen or missing at the time of the breach, the attacker must have used a stolen employee credential to gain access.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the security analyst's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The company's internal network monitoring system was functioning properly at the time of the breach.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The attacker did not gain access to the database by exploiting a software vulnerability that bypassed the credential and device requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Employee credentials are more frequently stolen than registered devices are reported missing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The company had not recently expanded the list of employees authorized to access the proprietary database.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The customer records exposed in the breach were the most sensitive data stored in the database.

explanations.correct: The analyst reasons that because no registered device was stolen, the attacker must have used a stolen credential. But this assumes the two-factor access requirements were the only way in. If the attacker bypassed both requirements through a software vulnerability, then neither a stolen device nor a stolen credential was needed. Negate B—the attacker did exploit such a vulnerability—and the conclusion evaporates. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Whether monitoring was functioning affects detection, not the mechanism of access. The argument is about how access was gained, not whether it was observed.
explanations.C: A comparative frequency claim is irrelevant to this specific breach; it would strengthen the argument at best but is not required for the conclusion.
explanations.D: Whether the authorized-user list expanded is out of scope; the argument concerns how the attacker got in, not who was legitimately authorized.
explanations.E: The sensitivity of the exposed records is irrelevant to how the breach was accomplished.

difficultyReason: The argument turns on a subtle sufficiency-of-evidence gap: ancient pollen deposits are used to date agricultural activity, but the necessary assumption concerns whether the pollen arrived via human cultivation rather than natural dispersal. Students often pick a too-strong distractor about all agriculture in the region.
stimulus: Archaeobotanist: Core samples taken from a peat bog in northern Europe contain cereal pollen deposits dating to approximately 4,800 years ago. Because cereal grasses are not native to this region and do not disperse their pollen over long distances, the presence of this pollen indicates that people were cultivating cereal crops near the bog at that time.
questionStem: The archaeobotanist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: no other archaeological sites in the region show evidence of agriculture predating 4,800 years ago.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the cereal pollen found in the bog was not transported there by traders passing through the region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: peat bogs are the most reliable repositories of ancient pollen deposits in northern Europe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the people cultivating cereal crops near the bog 4,800 years ago were permanent settlers rather than nomadic farmers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cereal grasses had not been introduced to the region earlier than 4,800 years ago by migratory birds.

explanations.correct: The argument's key premise is that cereal pollen doesn't disperse over long distances, so its presence implies local cultivation. But if traders carrying cereal grain passed through and deposited pollen—e.g., from stored grain—the pollen could be present without local cultivation. Negate B: the pollen was transported by traders. Then local cultivation is no longer established. The argument requires B.
explanations.A: Earlier sites elsewhere are irrelevant to whether this pollen indicates local cultivation 4,800 years ago; out of scope.
explanations.C: Peat bogs being the most reliable repository is a comparative claim not required for the conclusion; the argument uses this bog's data, not a claim about bogs generally.
explanations.D: Whether the farmers were nomadic or permanent is out of scope; the conclusion is only that people were cultivating crops nearby, not about their lifestyle.
explanations.E: Migratory birds could introduce live plants but not pollen deposits in the relevant sense; moreover, this would not undermine the premise that the pollen doesn't travel long distances on its own.

difficultyReason: The economic argument contains a conditional chain with a hidden assumption about market structure. The necessary assumption is a narrow defender ruling out a specific mechanism that would sever the causal link. Trap choices mimic the correct form but address different links in the chain.
stimulus: Economist: When the central bank raises the benchmark interest rate, commercial banks typically increase the rates they charge on consumer loans. Higher consumer loan rates reduce household borrowing. Reduced borrowing, in turn, leads to decreased consumer spending. Therefore, the central bank's recent rate increase will likely slow overall economic growth.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumer spending constitutes a sufficiently large share of the economy that a reduction in it would slow overall economic growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The central bank raises the benchmark interest rate only when inflation is above its target level.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commercial banks earn higher profits when the benchmark interest rate is elevated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Household borrowing is the primary driver of consumer spending in the economy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The central bank did not simultaneously implement other policies that would stimulate economic growth.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from decreased consumer spending to slowed overall economic growth. This step requires that consumer spending be a large enough component of the economy to affect overall growth. Negate A: consumer spending does not constitute a sufficiently large share—then reduced consumer spending would not slow overall growth, and the conclusion fails. A is necessary.
explanations.B: The reason the bank raises rates is irrelevant to whether the rate increase, once made, will slow growth through the described mechanism.
explanations.C: Bank profits are out of scope; the argument is about the effect on consumers and growth, not bank revenues.
explanations.D: Too strong—the argument requires only that reduced borrowing leads to decreased spending (as stated), not that borrowing is the primary driver of all consumer spending.
explanations.E: Simultaneous stimulative policies would undermine the conclusion, but the argument does not need to rule this out to establish the described causal chain; this is a strengthener, not a necessary assumption.

difficultyReason: The legal argument involves an evidentiary inference about intent. The necessary assumption rules out an alternative interpretation of a document—a subtle defender rather than a broad causal claim. Several traps address the legal standard rather than the logical gap.
stimulus: Attorney: The defendant signed a contract containing a clause that explicitly prohibited subletting the leased property. The defendant later sublet the property to a third party. My client, the property owner, is therefore entitled to damages, since the defendant cannot claim ignorance of the prohibition—the clause was clearly stated in the document the defendant signed.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the attorney's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The defendant understood the legal consequences of subletting at the time the contract was signed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Signing a contract constitutes sufficient evidence that the signer has read and understood its contents.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The property owner suffered measurable financial harm as a result of the subletting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The no-subletting clause is enforceable under the jurisdiction's contract law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defendant did not sublet the property under a reasonable belief that the property owner had given oral permission to do so.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument that the defendant cannot claim ignorance rests on the fact that the clause was in the signed document. This only defeats an ignorance defense if signing is taken as evidence of having read and understood the document. Negate B: signing does not constitute such evidence—then the defendant could still plausibly claim ignorance, and the attorney's specific rebuttal of that defense collapses. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Understanding legal consequences is a different matter from knowing about the prohibition; the argument is about awareness of the clause, not its legal ramifications.
explanations.C: The argument is about the defendant's knowledge and the contractual prohibition, not about whether damages are quantifiable; financial harm may be legally required but is not the logical gap the argument bridges.
explanations.D: Enforceability is a legal background condition, but the attorney's specific argument is about the ignorance defense—the logical gap is about notice, not enforceability per se.
explanations.E: Oral permission is a different defense not addressed in the argument; ruling it out would strengthen the case but is not required for the argument as stated.

difficultyReason: A linguistics argument about language change contains a subtle gap between synchronic evidence (current dialect features) and a diachronic conclusion (contact in the past). The necessary assumption concerns whether the shared feature originated in contact rather than independent development.
stimulus: Linguist: The dialect spoken in the coastal villages of this island shares seventeen phonological features with a dialect spoken in a region 400 kilometers away on the mainland. The probability of two dialects independently developing even a handful of such features is negligibly small. Therefore, the ancestors of the coastal villagers must have had sustained contact with speakers of the mainland dialect.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coastal villagers are currently aware of the linguistic similarities between their dialect and the mainland dialect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The seventeen shared phonological features were not all inherited from a common ancestral language spoken by both populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phonological features are more reliable indicators of language contact than grammatical features are.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coastal villagers' ancestors traveled to the mainland more frequently than mainland speakers traveled to the island.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The island's coastal villages were established before the mainland dialect developed its distinctive phonological features.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes the shared features to contact between the two populations. But shared features inherited from a common ancestor language would explain the similarities without any direct contact. Negate B: the features were all inherited from a common ancestral language—then the conclusion that the ancestors had sustained contact is unsupported. B is the necessary assumption.
explanations.A: Current awareness of the speakers is irrelevant to historical contact; out of scope.
explanations.C: A comparative reliability claim about feature types is not required; the argument uses phonological features and does not need to establish their superiority over other types.
explanations.D: The direction of travel is irrelevant to whether contact occurred at all; this is too specific and not required for the conclusion.
explanations.E: The chronological relationship between the villages and the mainland dialect's development is not part of the argument's reasoning chain.

difficultyReason: The medical argument uses a clinical trial result to draw a conclusion about mechanism. The necessary assumption is a narrow bridge ruling out an alternative mechanism (placebo effect) rather than confirming the drug's efficacy broadly. Students often choose a too-strong distractor about all patients.
stimulus: Clinical researcher: In our double-blind trial, patients who received the experimental compound showed a 40 percent reduction in inflammatory markers compared to those who received the placebo. Because the trial was double-blind, neither the patients nor the administering physicians knew who received the compound. We can therefore conclude that the compound itself, not patients' expectations of improvement, produced the reduction in inflammatory markers.
questionStem: The researcher's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inflammatory markers are the most accurate available measure of the condition the compound is intended to treat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The double-blind design prevented patients' expectations from differentially influencing inflammatory marker levels in the treatment group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All patients who received the compound experienced at least some reduction in inflammatory markers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The placebo used in the trial was chemically inert and had no therapeutic properties of its own.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who received the placebo did not experience any reduction in inflammatory markers.

explanations.correct: The researcher concludes that the compound—not patient expectations—caused the reduction. This relies on the double-blind design having successfully equalized expectations across both groups. If, despite the blinding, patients in the treatment group somehow formed stronger expectations of improvement (inflating the treatment effect), then patient expectation could still be responsible. Negate B: the double-blind design did not prevent differential expectation effects—then the conclusion that the compound itself caused the reduction is unsupported. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Whether inflammatory markers are the best measure is irrelevant to the causal attribution between the compound and those markers.
explanations.C: Too strong—the argument is about the group average, not that every single patient responded; requiring all patients to benefit is not part of the reasoning.
explanations.D: The placebo's inertness affects the interpretation of the control group's result but is not the logical gap the researcher's specific conclusion (compound vs. expectations) bridges.
explanations.E: Too strong—placebo patients could show some reduction and the conclusion would still hold, as long as the treatment group's greater reduction is attributed to the compound.

difficultyReason: An ethics argument about moral responsibility contains a hidden scope condition: the necessary assumption limits the principle invoked so that it doesn't overreach. The negation test requires identifying which limiting condition the argument silently depends on.
stimulus: Ethicist: A person is morally responsible for an outcome only if that person could reasonably have foreseen it. The engineers who designed the bridge followed all applicable safety codes and had no access to the geological data that would have revealed the unusual soil conditions contributing to the collapse. Therefore, the engineers bear no moral responsibility for the bridge's collapse.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The safety codes the engineers followed were adequate for most soil conditions likely to be encountered in bridge construction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Moral responsibility for an engineering failure cannot be distributed among multiple parties simultaneously.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The engineers could not reasonably have foreseen the bridge's collapse given the information available to them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The geological survey that would have revealed the unusual soil conditions was not required by the applicable safety codes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one who contributed to the bridge's design had access to the relevant geological data.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's principle is: moral responsibility requires reasonable foreseeability of the outcome. The conclusion is that the engineers bear no moral responsibility. To get there, the argument must establish that the engineers could not reasonably have foreseen the collapse. The premise says they followed codes and lacked the geological data, but the argument needs the further step that this means the collapse was not reasonably foreseeable. Negate C: the engineers could reasonably have foreseen the collapse—then even granting the principle, the engineers may bear moral responsibility. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Whether the codes were adequate for most conditions is background information, not the logical link needed to apply the principle to these engineers.
explanations.B: The argument is about these engineers specifically; whether responsibility can be shared is not required for the conclusion that they bear none.
explanations.D: Whether a geological survey was required is relevant to culpability under professional standards, not to the ethicist's specific foreseeability principle.
explanations.E: Too strong—even if some contributors had data, the argument concerns the specific engineers; but more importantly, the gap is about foreseeability, not about who had data.

difficultyReason: An arts-criticism argument uses provenance evidence to attribute a painting. The necessary assumption is a temporal defender—ruling out that the stylistic features were acquired after the artist's death through restoration—mirroring the lake-sediment anchor's chronological subtlety. Distractors address attribution criteria without targeting the temporal gap.
stimulus: Art historian: This unsigned painting depicts a scene and employs a color palette virtually identical to those in three works securely attributed to the seventeenth-century painter Vermeer. Dendrochronological analysis of the oak panel on which it is painted dates the panel to between 1650 and 1670—precisely Vermeer's most productive period. The painting must therefore be an authentic work by Vermeer.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the art historian's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vermeer painted more works on oak panels than on canvas during the period from 1650 to 1670.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other seventeenth-century painter used a color palette and compositional approach identical to Vermeer's.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stylistic features linking this painting to Vermeer's known works were not added by a later restorer who painted over an earlier composition on the panel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dendrochronological analysis of oak panels is accurate to within a margin of twenty years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vermeer signed the majority of the paintings he produced during his most productive period.

explanations.correct: The argument uses stylistic similarity plus panel dating to conclude Vermeer painted this work. The panel dates to Vermeer's era, but the stylistic features connecting it to Vermeer could have been applied by a later restorer who repainted an older panel in Vermeer's style. Negate C: the stylistic features were added by a later restorer—then the similarity to Vermeer's work does not establish that Vermeer was the artist, and the conclusion collapses. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Whether Vermeer preferred oak to canvas is irrelevant; the argument uses the dating, not a preference claim, to support the attribution.
explanations.B: Too strong—the argument requires that the combination of features points to Vermeer specifically, but ruling out every other seventeenth-century painter entirely is not the narrow assumption required; the argument could succeed even if a few others had similar styles.
explanations.D: The argument already uses a twenty-year date range, so the accuracy of the method within that range is a background premise, not the logical gap; moreover, even some imprecision wouldn't undermine the conclusion as long as the panel dates to roughly Vermeer's era.
explanations.E: The painting being unsigned is noted, not used as counter-evidence; whether Vermeer habitually signed works does not bridge the evidentiary gap the argument relies on.
